title: Regional processing and interpreting policy excerpts

opening.headline: In what region will data with different regulations differ from country to country be processed, and how will the legal provisions be read in conjunction with the service flow?
body: Inquiries from European customers may be processed using the model on US servers. Some customers request that their information be deleted, while others say they will view it. At this time, you can design the service flow by knowing how the regulatory provisions and product settings are connected.

In this lesson, we will first compare regional processing options provided by Anthropic API, Claude Enterprise, and Google Cloud. Next, we extract and read the definitions and principles of the GDPR, the data subject's rights, and the processor's obligations, followed by an explanation of how to match the provisions to the processing points of the service.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain regional processing options and key provisions of GDPR excerpts
The obligation to provide condolences can be matched to the AI service flow.

screens.title: Where is data processed with different regulations depending on the country?
screens.lead: Read the situations below and think about how you might connect regulations and product settings.

visual.alt: A flow chart showing how an inquiry from a European customer is sent to a model on a US server and a deletion request is sent back.

paragraphs: Inquiries from European customers are sent through our service to the model provider's servers. Regulatory review may vary depending on which country this server is located in. The same customer may one day request to view his or her information or request its deletion.

Regulators know the provisions, developers know the product settings. In order for both parties to understand what each other is saying, the condolences must be read in correspondence to indicate at which point in the service they are observed. This connection cannot be made by reading the full text from the beginning.
This class covers regional options and how to read GDPR excerpts into your service flow. It is not a substitute for legal advice, but rather a way to read the document and formulate questions.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: If a customer requests deletion, would it be enough to simply delete our database? The commentary follows where the data leads.

screens.outro: First, let's think about whether our work includes data with a defined processing area.

screens.title: Is there any work with a designated data processing area?
screens.lead: When you select a question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. The answer will not be submitted, so please think about our work first and then check.

items.prompt: Do you have a business that requires customer data to be processed only within a specific country?
items.answer: If you have a business with a specific processing area due to a contract or internal regulations, you should consider whether the location where the model call is made is also included in those conditions. The storage location and processing location may be different settings.

items.prompt: Do you know which region the AI service you use processes inference from?
items.answer: The default is often the way things can be done anywhere in the world. If you use it without knowing the default value, it may be processed in an unintended region, so you must first know the setting name and default value.

items.prompt: When a customer requests deletion, is there a standard for how far it must be deleted?
items.answer: Without criteria, only visible databases are usually deleted. We need a way to find the path leading to logs, memory, external providers, and the recipient of the data.

screens.outro: Now let’s look at regional processing options by product.

screens.title: Regional processing options
screens.lead: Select each tab to learn how processing regions are determined for each product. It is useful to note whether there are separate inference locations and storage locations.

tabs.label: Claude API
tabs.body: The Anthropic API has two settings that are independent of each other: The inference location (inference_geo) is determined for each request and is either global or us. global is the default and us runs inference only on US infrastructure. A workspace can have a list of allowed locations and a default location. The storage location (workspace geo) is where the data is saved. It is determined when creating the workspace and cannot be changed afterwards. Currently, only us can be selected. The usage in the response indicates the actual location of the inference.

tabs.label: Claude Enterprise
tabs.body: Claude Enterprise has an organizational unit setting called US-only inference. When turned on, inference for all apps, including Claude Code and Claude Desktop, will run on US servers, including background processing like conversation titles and memories. Available on the usage-based Enterprise plan and usage is billed at 1.1 times the standard rate. This setting does not change where your data is stored or processed by connected external services.

tabs.label: Google Cloud
tabs.body: Google Cloud's Agent Platform stores and processes data only in designated regions. The only exceptions are data labeling tasks and features in the experiment or preview stages. It also does not support global locations, so you must always specify a specific region. Generally, choose an area that is physically close or meets regulations.

tabs.label: reading tips
tabs.body: All three products have regional exceptions and scope limitations. When reading, check firstly whether inference and storage are separated, secondly whether the settings are per request or per organization, thirdly what functions are marked as exceptions, and fourthly whether they are handled separately by an external service. By organizing these four into the same column, you can compare products.

screens.outro: Now let's move on to how to read the legal text, starting with the definition and principles of GDPR.

screens.title: GDPR Excerpt: Definitions and Principles
screens.lead: When you hover over or select an underlined term in the text, an explanation appears. Check the key points of the provisions corresponding to definitions and principles one by one.

data.text: Article 4 of the GDPR defines personal data as any information relating to an identified individual or an identifiable individual, including indirect identifiers such as customer or reservation numbers. It also defines processing, controller, and processor. Article 5 establishes lawfulness, fairness and transparency; purpose limitation; Data Minimization; accuracy; storage limitation; integrity and confidentiality; and accountability. Information concerning health, biometrics, or political opinions is a special category of personal data. Its processing is generally prohibited unless an exception such as explicit consent applies. In an AI service, using a Customer name and number entered at the prompt already constitutes processing personal data.

terms.tip: It includes not only names but also identifiable individuals when combined with a number or other information.
The person who determines the purposes and means of processing personal information. This is usually the organization that operates our services.
A person who processes personal data on behalf of the controller. Model providers often take on this role.
The principle is that we only process personal information to the extent necessary for the purpose. This is directly related to the scope of personal information you enter in the prompt.
Sensitive information like health, biometrics, and political opinions are more protected. In principle, processing is prohibited and there must be grounds for exception.

terms.term: Customer name and number entered at the prompt
terms.tip: Personal data sent as input is also subject to processing. The mere fact that it is sent to a model does not mean it is not processed.

screens.outro: Now that you have read the principles, let us look at the data subject rights and processor obligations in order.

screens.title: GDPR Excerpt: Rights and Processor Obligations
screens.lead: Select the right arrow to read the condolences step by step. We will guide you through what kind of service each condolences is connected to.

steps.title: Article 12: How to respond to requests
steps.body: Requests from information subjects must be responded to transparently, and in principle, responses are made within one month. If your request is complex and difficult to process, you must notify us within one month. On the service side, procedures are needed to record the request receipt time and manage deadlines.

steps.title: Articles 15 and 17: Right to access and right to deletion
steps.body: Article 15 gives data subjects the right to view their information, and Article 17 gives data subjects the right to request deletion, the so-called right to be forgotten. The service side needs the ability to verify the requester's identity and find out what data is where.

steps.title: Article 19: Recipient Notification
steps.body: If you have made a correction or deletion, you must also notify the recipient of the personal information. Since the recipients may be external services or sub-services to which we have passed data, we need to have a list of where the data has been sent so that we can be notified.

steps.title: Article 28: Processor Obligations
steps.body: The controller should only use processors that provide sufficient guarantees, and the processor helps the controller process the data subject's requests. When using a model provider, we sign a processing contract and make sure this support is included in the contract.

steps.title: Article 35: Impact assessment
steps.body: A Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) must be carried out before any processing that may pose a high risk to the rights and freedoms of individuals. Build a step into your development process to consider whether this evaluation is necessary before releasing new AI features.

screens.outro: Now that you have read the clause, let us correspond to the service flow with an actual deletion request example.

screens.title: Commentary: How delete requests affect logs and memory
screens.lead: We will explain in four steps a case in which a European customer requested that the customer service erase his or her data. Select the next arrow to proceed.

steps.title: Step 1: Draw a data map
steps.body: When we receive a request, we first find out where that customer's data is. Find and catalog all conversation records, inputs sent to model providers, internal logs, and the service's memory storage. This step sets the scope for subsequent steps, as you cannot delete places that are not on the list.

steps.title: Step 2: Delete from our side
steps.body: It erases the places we control: conversation history and memory storage, and leaves behind a record of our processing. If the original text remains in the log, the log is also eligible. Be sure to record the fact that you deleted it and the date and time so you can explain it later.

steps.title: Step 3: Check with the provider
steps.body: Check when deleted conversations in the provider's documents are deleted from the backend and whether a separate abuse monitoring log is left. For example, some providers state that any conversation you delete from the screen will be deleted from the backend within 30 days. We will inform the requester exactly what we cannot erase immediately.

steps.title: Step 4: Inform the recipient and respond
steps.body: We notify the external service that received the data of the deletion, and respond to the requester with the results within one month. In your response, write down what you erased, what remained, and why. If there is any remaining data, it is appropriate for transparency to disclose the retention period as well.

screens.outro: Now, we will organize the obligations of each article into a table corresponding to the processing point of the service flow.

screens.title: Explanation: Table matching condolences to service flow
screens.lead: This table pairs processing points for condolences and services. Read each line to see if there is a corresponding point in our service.

data.notes: Blank cells in the table indicate obligations that do not yet have a processing point in our service. You can fill in the rows that do not answer the inspection questions in order of priority. This table is not legal advice, but rather a tool for reading articles in relation to service flows. After filling out the table, add the department in charge and the name of the supporting document in each row one by one so that it can be inherited even if the person in charge changes.

screens.outro: Now that I have created a table, I will organize the class.

screens.title: Key takeaway: condolences are read in correspondence to the service flow
screens.lead: Summarizes the contents of this class.

paragraphs: Regional processing is set and confirmed by dividing the inference location and storage location. You should also check whether the unit of setting is a request or an organization, what functions are listed as exceptions, and whether external services handle them separately. Even if you specify a region, some system data or features may be out of scope.

The GDPR is read in the following order: definitions, principles, rights and processor obligations. If you map the table to show at which point in the service the condolence is kept, you will see an empty processing point. Delete requests are followed through logs, memory, external providers, and recipients by creating a data map.

The most practical way to prepare is to decide who handles where and when a rights request comes in. Rather than reading the entire statement, read the statement that corresponds to our service flow first. Even after the correspondence table is created once, the number of rows increases each time a new feature is added. By managing all three together – zoning, response tables, and data maps – regulators and developers can talk to each other on the same page.

callout.label: Points to remember
callout.text: This class is not legal advice, but rather how to read documents and formulate questions.

checks.intro: Check out the structure of your regional settings yourself. This confirmation is not logged.
checks.q: What are the appropriate inference location and storage location settings for Anthropic API?
options: Both can be changed on request
The storage location is fixed for each request, and the inference location is fixed when creating a workspace.
The inference location is determined for each request, and the storage location is determined when creating a workspace and cannot be changed.
Both are fixed at the time of workspace creation and cannot be changed.
checks.explain: The inference location (inference_geo) can be set to global or us for each request, and the storage location is set when creating the workspace and cannot be changed afterward.

wrong.0: The storage location cannot be changed after creation.
wrong.1: The locking method for both settings is reversed.
wrong.3: Inference locations can be specified on a per-request basis.

checks.correctFeedback: That's right. The two settings are independent and have different fixation methods.
checks.incorrectFeedback: The locking method of both settings is mixed. Recall which settings are per-request.

checks.intro: Match processing points in condolences and service flows. For each condolence on the left, select the appropriate point on the right.
checks.q: Match the following GDPR provisions with processing points in your service flow:
left: Articles 15 and 17 Right to view and delete
right: Scope of personal information entered in the prompt
checks.explain: If you map to which point in the service the condolence is kept, you will see the missing processing point.
checks.correctFeedback: I've linked all four condolences to the appropriate points. The responsiveness of condolences and service flow is clear.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Some connections are off. Divide the obligations observed at the input stage and those observed at the request processing stage.

glossary.def: Specifies the geographic location where data is processed and stored.
This parameter specifies, per request, the region where inference is run in the Claude API.
The person who determines the purpose and means of processing and the person who processes it on his or her behalf. They have different duties.
These are the rights you have regarding your personal information, such as viewing, correction, and deletion.
Data protection impact assessment before high-risk processing.

misconceptions.myth: If you specify a region, all data resides only in that region.
misconceptions.fact: System data or some features may be out of your region. You should read the exceptions in the documentation together.

misconceptions.myth: A deletion request only requires deleting our database.
misconceptions.fact: You have to keep up with external providers, logs, memory, and even recipient notifications.

misconceptions.myth: The entire provision must be read.
misconceptions.fact: It is more practical to read the condolences that correspond to the service flow first.

closing.lead: We recapitulate the key points of this lesson.
points: Local options split inference and storage.
The GDPR reads in the following order: Definitions, Principles, Rights and Processor Obligations.
Condolences are matched with service points and tickets.
Deletion requests are tracked with a data map.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for your own reflection only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: When a customer's view/delete request comes in from our service, who handles it at which point and which part is empty?
